q: The 2025 Lancet Commission split obesity into which two categories?
src: Lancet Diab Endo Commission 2025
exp: The 2025 Lancet Commission split obesity into clinical obesity, where excess fat already harms organ function, and preclinical obesity, where function is still preserved.

q: Under the Lancet Commission, what defines clinical obesity?
a: Organ dysfunction or functional limitation caused by excess adiposity
BMI above 30 plus an elevated waist circumference
Body weight above 120% of ideal weight
A family history of obesity-related disease
src: Lancet Commission 2025
exp: The defining feature is not the weight number but organ dysfunction or limitation of daily life caused by excess adiposity.

q: What is preclinical obesity?
a: Excess adiposity with preserved organ function
Normal fat mass with low muscle mass
The early phase where organ dysfunction has begun
src: Lancet Commission 2025
exp: Preclinical obesity means excess fat with normal organ function, so it calls for risk management and monitoring rather than treatment.

q: Why did the Commission say BMI alone should not diagnose obesity?
a: BMI does not directly capture the amount or distribution of body fat
The BMI formula has to be recalculated for each ethnic group
BMI cannot be adjusted for age or sex in adults
BMI needs body-composition equipment to calculate
src: Lancet Commission 2025
exp: BMI shows neither how much fat there is nor where it sits, so it cannot separate a muscular person from one with visceral fat.

q: Besides BMI, what does the Commission require to confirm excess adiposity?
a: A fat measure such as waist circumference, waist-hip or waist-height ratio
Fasting glucose and HbA1c to confirm metabolic disease
Blood pressure and LDL cholesterol to confirm cardiovascular risk
Liver enzyme (ALT) levels to confirm liver involvement
src: Lancet Commission 2025
exp: That is why at least one fat-distribution measure such as waist circumference, waist-hip or waist-height ratio should be added to BMI.

q: Which waist-to-height ratio threshold suggests central adiposity?
src: EASO framework 2024
exp: A waist larger than half the height (ratio above 0.5) signals excess abdominal fat.

q: In Korea, obesity is defined from which BMI?
src: Korean Society for the Study of Obesity
exp: Western cut-offs use 30, but Asians develop metabolic disease at lower BMI, so Korea defines obesity from 25.

q: In the Korean criteria, pre-obesity (overweight) starts at which BMI?
src: KSSO guideline
exp: BMI 23–24.9 is the pre-obesity range where metabolic risk starts to climb.

q: Korean class 3 (severe) obesity starts at which BMI?
src: KSSO guideline
exp: Korean classes are 25–29.9 (class 1), 30–34.9 (class 2) and 35 or more (class 3).

q: Why is metabolic risk higher in Asians at the same BMI?
a: A higher share of visceral fat at the same body weight
More muscle mass than Western populations
src: WHO Asia-Pacific / KSSO
exp: At the same weight Asians carry a larger share of visceral fat, so insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction appear more easily.

q: How should obesity be regarded?
a: A chronic disease with frequent relapse
An acute condition cured by lifestyle change
A congenital disorder determined only by genes
A condition that does not recur after weight loss
src: Lancet Commission 2025 / WHO
exp: Obesity is a chronic, relapsing disease rather than a matter of willpower, so it needs long-term care.

q: What is the first benefit expected from 5-10% weight loss?
a: Improvement in comorbidity markers such as glucose, blood pressure and triglycerides
Structural regeneration of knee joint cartilage
A significant rise in basal metabolic rate
Higher bone density and lower fracture risk
src: AHA/ACC/TOS Guideline
exp: Even a 5–10% loss improves comorbidity markers such as glucose, blood pressure and triglycerides first.

q: Why is visceral (central) adiposity especially harmful?
a: Free fatty acids drain through the portal vein into the liver and drive metabolic dysfunction
Its fat cells are smaller and store less lipid than subcutaneous fat cells
It secretes more leptin, which suppresses appetite and lowers intake
It accumulates around muscle and directly reduces muscle strength
src: Portal theory / KSSO
exp: Free fatty acids from visceral fat drain through the portal vein straight into the liver, driving insulin resistance and fatty liver.

q: What should be protected during weight loss?
src: Obesity management guidelines
exp: Losing muscle along with fat lowers metabolic rate and invites regain, so protein intake and resistance training protect lean mass.

q: What is the foundation of every obesity treatment plan?
a: Lifestyle intervention: diet, exercise and behavioural therapy
Monthly liver and kidney function tests throughout treatment
A low-calorie meal replacement used on its own
An antidepressant added from the start of treatment
src: Obesity guidelines
exp: Whatever treatment is chosen, diet, exercise and behavioural therapy are the base on which everything else is built.

q: What BMI generally triggers consideration of metabolic/bariatric surgery?
a: BMI 35 or higher, or 30 or higher with comorbidities
BMI 30 or higher regardless of comorbidities
src: ASMBS/IFSO 2022
exp: Surgery is considered at BMI 35 or higher regardless of comorbidity, and at 30 or higher with metabolic disease.

q: Which cancer is NOT among those linked to obesity?
src: IARC / WHO
exp: Obesity raises the risk of colorectal, postmenopausal breast, endometrial and other cancers, but melanoma is not on that list.

q: Which sleep disorder commonly accompanies obesity?
src: Obesity comorbidity
exp: Fat around the neck and upper airway narrows it, so obstructive sleep apnoea is common in obesity.

q: How does weight loss affect steatotic liver disease (MASLD)?
a: 5–7% loss improves inflammation and 7–10% can improve fibrosis
Steatosis improves only after a loss of 15% or more
Only exercise helps, regardless of weight
src: Vilar-Gomez 2015 / AASLD
exp: Inflammation improves with 5–7% loss and fibrosis with 7–10%, which is why weight loss is the core of fatty-liver care.

q: What should clinicians avoid when caring for patients with obesity?
src: Weight stigma consensus 2020
exp: Blaming willpower stigmatises patients and drives them away from care; obesity should be treated as a disease.

q: What metabolic adaptation follows weight loss?
a: Energy expenditure falls and appetite hormones rise, pushing weight back up
Basal metabolic rate rises so further loss gets easier
Thyroid hormone rises and increases heat production
src: Metabolic adaptation research
exp: After loss, energy expenditure falls and appetite hormones rise, pushing the body back toward its old weight, so a maintenance plan is essential.

q: Which joint problem commonly accompanies obesity?
src: Obesity comorbidity
exp: Load on the knee cartilage makes knee osteoarthritis the most common joint problem.

q: What is a safe, sustainable rate of weight loss?
src: Obesity guidelines
exp: 0.5–1 kg a week is a sustainable pace that preserves muscle.

q: How should cardiovascular risk in obesity be reduced?
a: Manage weight together with blood pressure, lipids and glucose
Treat blood pressure first and leave weight for later
No further management if a cardiac work-up is normal
src: CKM syndrome (AHA 2023)
exp: Weight loss alone is not enough; blood pressure, lipids and glucose must be managed together to lower cardiovascular risk.

q: In the AHA cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) framework, where does obesity sit?
a: The starting point: excess or dysfunctional adipose tissue in the earliest stage
Stage 2, which comes after kidney damage has developed
Stage 4, which comes after cardiovascular disease has occurred
It is not included in the CKM staging at all
src: AHA CKM advisory 2023
exp: The AHA places excess or dysfunctional adipose tissue at stage 1, the starting point of CKM syndrome.

q: What is the main role of exercise in weight management?
a: Maintaining lost weight and preserving muscle
Producing large weight loss without dietary change
Reducing subcutaneous rather than visceral fat
src: Obesity guidelines
exp: Exercise rarely produces large loss on its own, but it is central to keeping weight off and preserving muscle.

q: According to the KSSO 2025 Obesity Fact Sheet, what was the adult obesity prevalence (BMI ≥25) in Korea in 2023?
src: KSSO 2025 Obesity Fact Sheet — 38.4% in 2023
exp: Adult obesity prevalence in Korea was 38.4% in 2023, about four in ten adults.

q: Per the 2025 fact sheet, what was the obesity prevalence among adult men in 2023?
src: KSSO 2025 Obesity Fact Sheet — men 49.8%
exp: Among men it was 49.8%, one in two.

q: Per the 2025 fact sheet, what was the obesity prevalence among adult women in 2023?
src: KSSO 2025 Obesity Fact Sheet — women 27.5%
exp: Among women it was 27.5%, about half the male rate but still more than one in four.

q: What trend in adult obesity prevalence over the last three years did the 2025 fact sheet highlight?
a: It is rising about 2 points a year
It has turned into a clear decline
src: KSSO 2025 Obesity Fact Sheet — plateau over 3 years
exp: After rising for a decade, prevalence has plateaued around 38% for three years, the first positive signal.

q: Per the 2025 fact sheet, what was the prevalence of abdominal obesity (waist ≥90 cm men / ≥85 cm women) in 2023?
src: KSSO 2025 Obesity Fact Sheet — abdominal obesity 24.3%
exp: Abdominal obesity was 24.3%, one in four adults: 31.3% of men and 17.7% of women.

q: Which age band had the highest obesity prevalence in 2023?
src: KSSO 2025 Obesity Fact Sheet — 30s 42.0%, 40s 42.2%
exp: Prevalence peaks in the 30s (42.0%) and 40s (42.2%), the prime working years.

q: What waist-circumference cut-offs define abdominal obesity in Koreans according to KSSO?
a: ≥90 cm in men, ≥85 cm in women
≥94 cm in men, ≥80 cm in women
≥102 cm in men, ≥88 cm in women
≥85 cm in men, ≥80 cm in women
src: KSSO 2025 Obesity Fact Sheet / KSSO guideline
exp: KSSO defines abdominal obesity as a waist of 90 cm or more in men and 85 cm or more in women.

q: Per the Diabetes Fact Sheet 2024, what was diabetes prevalence among Koreans aged 30 or older in 2022?
src: KDA Diabetes Fact Sheet in Korea 2024 — 14.8% in 2022
exp: In 2022, 14.8% of adults aged 30 or older had diabetes: one in seven, about 5.3 million people.

q: What is the prevalence of diabetes among Koreans aged 65 or older?
src: KDA Diabetes Fact Sheet in Korea 2024 — ages 65+: 28–30%
exp: Among people aged 65 or older, 28–30% have diabetes, three in ten.

q: What share of Koreans aged 30 or older have prediabetes (fasting glucose 100–125 or HbA1c 5.7–6.4%)?
src: KDA Diabetes Fact Sheet in Korea 2024 — 41.1%, 14 million
exp: Prediabetes affects 41.1%, about 14 million people, nearly three times the number with diabetes.

q: What share of people with diabetes also had obesity (BMI ≥25)?
src: KDA Diabetes Fact Sheet in Korea 2024 — obesity 53.8%
exp: 53.8% of people with diabetes have obesity (BMI ≥25), so weight and glucose management go together.

q: What share of people with diabetes also had abdominal obesity?
src: KDA Diabetes Fact Sheet in Korea 2024 — abdominal obesity 61.2%
exp: 61.2% of people with diabetes have abdominal obesity, more often women.

q: Which of the following is NOT part of the fact sheet definition of diabetes?
src: KDA Diabetes Fact Sheet in Korea 2024 — definition of diabetes
exp: Fasting glucose 100–125 defines prediabetes; diabetes means ≥126, HbA1c ≥6.5%, a physician diagnosis or drug treatment.

q: How did the Lancet Commission say BMI should be used when diagnosing obesity?
a: Only as a screening tool; confirmation needs a measure of body fat
BMI should not be used at all
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: BMI is only a screening tool; confirmation needs a fat-distribution measure such as waist circumference or direct measurement.

q: When can excess adiposity be assumed without additional measurements under the Commission criteria?
a: When only waist circumference is measured
When there is a family history
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: Above BMI 40 excess adiposity is virtually certain, so no further measurement is required.

q: Which of these are examples of organ dysfunction that count toward clinical obesity?
a: Fatty liver, sleep apnoea, knee pain with reduced function
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: Findings such as fatty liver, sleep apnoea and impaired knee function show that excess fat has altered organ function.

q: Besides organ dysfunction, what other criterion can establish clinical obesity?
a: Significant, age-adjusted limitation of mobility or basic daily activities
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: Even without test findings, significant limitation of mobility or basic daily activities can establish clinical obesity.

q: What management did the Commission recommend for preclinical obesity?
a: Counselling, monitoring and lifestyle management to reduce risk
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: Preclinical obesity is a risk state rather than a disease, so the goal is counselling, monitoring and lifestyle care to prevent progression.

q: How did the Commission define the goal of treating clinical obesity?
a: Improving or achieving remission of organ dysfunction and preventing complications
Only bringing the weight number back to a normal BMI
Maximising the speed of weight loss
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: The goal is not a weight number but improvement or remission of organ dysfunction and prevention of complications.

q: How did the Lancet Commission characterise clinical obesity?
a: A chronic systemic illness in which excess adiposity alters organ function
A temporary state created by lifestyle
A congenital disorder determined only by genes
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: The Commission defined clinical obesity as a chronic systemic illness in which excess fat alters organ function.

q: What did the Commission recommend regarding weight stigma?
a: Training for clinicians and policymakers to address weight-based bias and stigma
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: It recommended training for clinicians and policymakers to reduce weight-based bias and stigma.

q: Which cluster forms the "metabolic" criterion for clinical obesity?
a: Hyperglycaemia together with high triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol
High uric acid with low calcium
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: The metabolic criterion is hyperglycaemia together with high triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol.

q: Which findings belong to the cardiovascular criteria for clinical obesity?
a: Heart failure, atrial fibrillation, raised blood pressure
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: Cardiovascular criteria include heart failure, atrial fibrillation and raised blood pressure.

q: What is the key distinction between clinical and preclinical obesity?
a: Whether organ dysfunction or limitation of daily activities is present
src: Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission 2025 (clinical obesity)
exp: What separates the two is not weight but whether organ dysfunction or limitation of daily life is present.

q: What first-line treatment goal does the KSSO guideline recommend?
a: Losing 5–10% of initial body weight within 6 months
Continuing until a normal BMI is reached
Gaining muscle without any weight change
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: KSSO recommends losing 5–10% of initial weight within 6 months as the first goal.

q: How often does the KSSO guideline advise adults to have BMI measured?
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: Every adult should have BMI measured yearly: 23 or more is pre-obesity, 25 or more is obesity.

q: What daily calorie reduction does the guideline recommend for a low-calorie diet?
a: A deficit of 500–1,000 kcal a day (0.5–1 kg loss a week)
A deficit of 100 kcal a day
A deficit of 2,000 kcal a day
Skipping one meal entirely each day
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: A 500–1,000 kcal daily deficit gives 0.5–1 kg a week, with the biggest effect in the first 6 months.

q: What exercise prescription does the guideline recommend for weight loss?
a: At least 150 minutes of aerobic exercise a week plus resistance training 2–3 times a week
One high-intensity session a week only
Ten minutes of stretching daily only
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: At least 150 minutes of aerobic exercise plus resistance training 2–3 times a week preserves muscle while losing weight.

q: Under the Korean guideline, when may pharmacotherapy for obesity be considered?
a: BMI ≥25 with failure of non-drug treatment
Whenever the patient wishes, regardless of BMI
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: The Korean guideline considers pharmacotherapy as an add-on at BMI 25 or higher when lifestyle change has failed.

q: What does the guideline recommend to keep weight off after loss?
a: Continue a high-protein, low-fat diet with exercise and check weight regularly
Lift all dietary limits after losing weight
Put the scale away and go by feel
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: A high-protein, low-fat diet with continued exercise, regular weigh-ins and professional feedback keeps the weight off.

q: Which measure is combined with BMI in the KSSO comorbidity-risk table?
a: Waist circumference (≥90 cm men / ≥85 cm women raises the risk category)
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: At the same BMI, a waist of 90/85 cm or more moves the comorbidity risk up one category.

q: What should be checked at the first visit to rule out secondary obesity?
a: Conditions that raise weight (hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome) and current medications
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: Rule out secondary obesity first by checking conditions such as hypothyroidism or Cushing syndrome and weight-gaining medications.

q: At what age does the KDA 2023 guideline recommend starting diabetes screening?
a: All adults aged 35 or older (19 or older with risk factors)
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: The 2023 guideline recommends screening all adults from 35, and from 19 when risk factors are present.

q: Which item was newly added to the diabetes-screening risk factors in the 2023 guideline?
a: Abdominal obesity (waist ≥90 cm men / ≥85 cm women)
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: Because abdominal obesity and diabetes are rising in younger adults, abdominal obesity was added as a screening risk factor.

q: How much weight loss does the KDA 2023 guideline recommend for overweight or obese adults with diabetes?
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: Overweight or obese adults with diabetes should lose at least 5% and maintain it by cutting total calories.

q: How much exercise is recommended for people with diabetes?
a: At least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise a week plus resistance exercise twice a week or more
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: At least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise plus resistance training twice a week is the standard prescription.

q: What lifestyle target is recommended to prevent progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes?
a: 5–7% weight loss and at least 150 minutes of exercise a week
Weight maintenance and 30 minutes of exercise a week
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: In prediabetes, 5–7% weight loss and 150 minutes of exercise a week cut the risk of diabetes by more than half.

q: What is the general HbA1c target for adults with type 2 diabetes in the Korean guideline?
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: The KDA general HbA1c target is below 6.5%, adjusted for the individual.

q: Which of the following is NOT a diagnostic criterion for diabetes?
a: 2-hour glucose ≥200 mg/dL on a 75 g OGTT
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: Diabetes is diagnosed by fasting glucose ≥126, HbA1c ≥6.5% or a 2-hour OGTT value ≥200; 110 falls in the prediabetes range.

q: How should fatty liver be viewed in people with type 2 diabetes?
a: It is very common and carries a higher risk of fibrosis, so it should be assessed
It is rare and need not be checked
Normal liver enzymes rule it out
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes / KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline
exp: Fatty liver is very common in type 2 diabetes and more likely to progress to fibrosis, so it should be assessed.

q: What is the simplest way to identify abdominal obesity?
a: Measuring waist circumference with a tape
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: A tape measure around the waist is the simplest validated way to identify abdominal obesity.

q: Where and how should waist circumference be measured?
a: Midway between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone, after breathing out
At the narrowest point while breathing in
5 cm below the navel over clothing
At the widest part of the hips
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: Measure horizontally midway between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone after breathing out.

q: What is the most effective way to reduce visceral fat?
a: Calorie restriction with regular aerobic and resistance exercise
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: Visceral fat responds best to calorie restriction with aerobic and resistance exercise; spot exercises do not remove it.

q: What can a person with type 2 diabetes and obesity expect from losing 5–10% of body weight?
a: Better insulin sensitivity and lower glucose and HbA1c
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: A 5–10% loss improves insulin sensitivity and lowers glucose and HbA1c, and larger losses can lead to remission.

q: Which statement about fatty liver and type 2 diabetes is correct?
a: They raise each other's risk in both directions
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline
exp: Fatty liver roughly doubles the risk of diabetes, and diabetes speeds the progression of fatty liver, a two-way relationship.

q: When a person with type 2 diabetes has fatty liver, what should be checked in particular?
a: Whether fibrosis has developed (non-invasive markers such as FIB-4)
src: KASL 2025 MASLD Clinical Practice Guideline
exp: Fibrosis, not fat itself, determines prognosis, so FIB-4 or similar markers are used to gauge fibrosis risk first.

q: How does body-fat distribution change after menopause?
a: Visceral fat increases and abdominal obesity becomes more common
Only subcutaneous fat rises while visceral fat falls
Body fat falls on its own
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: Falling oestrogen after menopause shifts fat from hips and thighs to the abdomen.

q: In which group has obesity risen most steeply in Korea over the past decade?
src: KSSO 2025 Obesity Fact Sheet
exp: Obesity among men in their 20s rose from 32% to 45% in a decade, the steepest increase of any group.

q: What needs special attention when managing obesity in older adults?
a: Preventing sarcopenic obesity by combining resistance exercise with adequate protein
Losing as much weight as fast as possible
src: KSSO Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline 2022 (8th ed)
exp: Older adults lose muscle easily during weight loss, so resistance training and adequate protein prevent sarcopenic obesity.

q: Which statement describes young-adult (19–39) diabetes in Korea?
a: Obesity is very common (nine in ten) and diagnosis and treatment rates are low
Control rates are higher than in the elderly
It is far more common in women
src: KDA Diabetes Fact Sheet in Korea 2024
exp: Nine in ten young adults with diabetes have obesity, and awareness (43%) and treatment (35%) are the lowest of any age group.

q: What should a woman do after a pregnancy with gestational diabetes?
a: Have regular glucose testing because the risk of type 2 diabetes is high
No testing is needed because the risk ends with delivery
Test only during the next pregnancy
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: Gestational diabetes greatly raises later type 2 diabetes risk, so regular glucose testing continues after delivery.

q: Why does obesity matter so much in adults with diabetes?
a: More than half of people with diabetes have obesity, and it makes glucose, blood pressure and lipid control harder
Obesity is rare in people with diabetes
src: KDA 2023 Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diabetes
exp: More than half of people with diabetes have obesity, which makes glucose, blood pressure and lipid control all harder.

q: Why does adult body weight stay stable for years despite large daily swings in intake and activity?
a: Because body weight is homeostatically regulated, centred on the hypothalamus
Because calorie intake is the same every day
src: Pasquet P, Apfelbaum M. Am J Clin Nutr 1994 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 1)
exp: The hypothalamus integrates signals such as leptin and ghrelin to balance intake and expenditure, keeping weight stable.

q: Where is leptin produced and what does it do?
a: It is made by fat cells and suppresses appetite
It is made by the stomach and triggers hunger
It is made by the pancreas and raises glucose
It is made by the liver and stores fat
src: Zhang Y et al. Nature 1994; Considine RV et al. N Engl J Med 1996 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 1)
exp: Leptin from fat cells tells the hypothalamus the body is well fed and suppresses appetite.

q: Which statement about ghrelin is correct?
a: It is released from the stomach and stimulates hunger
It is released from fat cells and suppresses appetite
It is released from muscle and raises heat production
It is released from the kidney and regulates water
src: Wren AM et al. Endocrinology 2000 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 1)
exp: Ghrelin is the hunger hormone from the stomach that rises before meals.

q: What is the typical course after lifestyle-induced weight loss?
a: Loss peaks at 6–12 months and by 5 years most people are back at their starting weight
Loss continues and people are lighter at 5 years
Once lost, weight is mostly kept for life
Everything is regained within a month
src: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Overweight and Obesity 2013 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 1)
exp: Loss peaks at 6–12 months, most is regained within 2 years and most people are back at baseline by 5 years, so maintenance is key.

q: What happens to energy expenditure after a 10% weight loss?
a: It falls below what the new body size predicts and the drop persists
It returns to normal within a week
src: Rosenbaum M, Leibel RL. Obesity 2016; Fothergill E et al. Obesity 2016 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 1)
exp: After a 10% loss, expenditure falls below what the new weight predicts and the change persists.

q: One year after weight loss, how does hunger compare with before?
a: It is still higher than before the loss
It returns to the pre-loss level
src: Sumithran P et al. N Engl J Med 2011 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 1)
exp: A year after weight loss, hunger and appetite hormones remain higher than before the loss.

q: What did the study overfeeding 12 pairs of identical twins by about 1,000 kcal/day for 100 days show?
a: Weight gain was similar within each twin pair, pointing to genetic influence
Everyone gained exactly the same amount
src: Bouchard C et al. N Engl J Med 1990 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 2)
exp: Twins gained similar amounts within pairs but differed widely between pairs, showing a strong genetic effect on weight gain.

q: In the Danish adoption study, whose weight did adult adoptees resemble?
src: Stunkard AJ et al. N Engl J Med 1986 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 2)
exp: Adoptees resembled their biological rather than adoptive parents, showing the influence of genes.

q: What characterises weight gain at menopause?
a: Visceral fat rises and gain is central (abdominal)
It goes only to hips and thighs
src: Lovejoy JC et al. Int J Obes 2008 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 2)
exp: Menopausal weight gain is centred on visceral fat, so the waist expands first.

q: Which of these is NOT a medical cause of weight gain?
src: Nieman LK et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2008 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 2)
exp: Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss; Cushing syndrome, hypothalamic injury and Prader–Willi syndrome cause gain.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the five components of the metabolic syndrome?
src: Alberti KG et al. Circulation 2009 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: The five criteria are waist circumference, triglycerides, HDL, blood pressure and glucose; BMI is not one of them.

q: How many of the five risk factors are needed to diagnose the metabolic syndrome?
src: Alberti KG et al. Circulation 2009 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: Three or more of the five risk factors make the diagnosis.

q: What share of women with PCOS have obesity?
src: Azziz R et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2006 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: 50–80% of women with PCOS have obesity, and weight loss improves both ovulation and metabolism.

q: Which statement about PCOS and metabolic health is correct?
a: It is linked to insulin resistance and a higher risk of type 2 diabetes
src: Azziz R et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2006 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: PCOS is closely tied to insulin resistance and raises the risk of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.

q: What is the strongest predictor of obstructive sleep apnoea?
src: Epstein LJ et al. (AASM Task Force) J Clin Sleep Med 2009 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: Obesity is the strongest predictor of sleep apnoea, ahead of age, sex or hypertension.

q: In the STOP-BANG sleep-apnoea screen, what does the B stand for?
src: Chung F et al. Anesthesiology 2008 (STOP-BANG) (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 3)
exp: In STOP-BANG, B is BMI over 35, A age over 50, N neck over 40 cm and G male gender.

q: What does "BMI tells you how big your patient is" imply?
a: How sick they are needs a separate staging tool such as EOSS
A higher BMI always means sicker
src: Sharma AM, Kushner RF. Int J Obes 2009 (Edmonton Obesity Staging System) (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 4)
exp: BMI only tells you size; actual health impact needs a staging tool such as EOSS.

q: Which predicts survival better in people with obesity?
a: A staging system that reflects organ damage (EOSS)
src: Padwal RS et al. CMAJ 2011 (EOSS and mortality) (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 4)
exp: EOSS staging, which reflects organ damage, predicts survival far better than BMI class.

q: Which is NOT one of the "4Ms" of obesity assessment?
src: Sharma AM. Obes Rev 2010 (the 4Ms) (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 4)
exp: The 4Ms are Mental, Mechanical, Monetary and Metabolic, a frame for causes, complications and barriers.

q: What is the right way to raise weight during a consultation?
a: Deal with the presenting problem first, then raise weight, linked to it where possible
Point out the weight in the first sentence so it is not forgotten
Set the presenting complaint aside and talk only about weight
Never mention weight until the patient does
src: Vallis M et al. Can Fam Physician 2013 (5As of obesity management) (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 4)
exp: Handle the presenting problem first and link weight to it where possible so the conversation stays open.

q: Roughly how many kilocalories does 1 kg of body fat represent?
src: Wishnofsky M. Am J Clin Nutr 1958 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 6)
exp: One kilogram of fat is about 7,000 kcal, so a 500 kcal daily deficit removes about 1 kg in two weeks.

q: What did the 2-year trial of 811 adults on four diets with different fat, protein and carbohydrate shares conclude?
a: With calories reduced, weight loss was similar whatever the macronutrient mix
The high-carbohydrate diet caused weight gain
Nobody lost weight on any diet
src: Sacks FM et al. N Engl J Med 2009 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 6)
exp: In 811 adults over two years, weight loss was similar whatever the macronutrient mix, showing that calorie reduction is what matters.

q: How did intermittent calorie restriction (e.g. 5:2) compare with daily restriction?
a: Similar weight loss; a matter of what suits the person
src: Harvie MN et al. Int J Obes 2011 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 6)
exp: Intermittent restriction such as 5:2 works about as well as daily restriction, so choose what fits the person.

q: What is the main value of exercise in weight management?
a: Limiting muscle loss during weight loss and keeping the weight off
Producing large loss without dietary change
src: Donnelly JE et al. (ACSM position stand) Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 6)
exp: Exercise matters less for the loss itself than for limiting muscle loss and keeping the weight off.

q: What is described as the hardest part of obesity treatment?
a: Keeping weight off long term — obesity is a chronic condition needing lifelong care
src: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines 2013 (cited in SCOPE Core Learning Path, module 6)
exp: Keeping weight off long term is the hard part, which is why obesity is treated as a chronic condition needing lifelong care.
